CASSI-Lite: A Resource-Efficient OCR and
Concept-Aware Framework for Plagiarism
Detection
Anshu Kumar1, Anirban Dutta2, Purushottam Choudhary3, and Amit Seth∗4
1,2,3,4Department of Computer Science & Engineering
1,2,3,4Sharda University, Greater Noida, India
anshuukumar2910@gmail.com,anirban311004@gmail.com
purushottamchoudhary2910@gmail.com,amitseth.it@gmail.com
Abstract.

The generative AI and image editing software have been de-
mocratized and introduced advanced plagiarism avoidance techniques
rendering the existing text-matching algorithms obsolete.

Image manip-
ulation (snapshots), embedded scanned texts, or Large Language Models
(LLM) can now be used by students and researchers to avoid the detec-
tion of plagiarism by paraphrasing text without changing the underly-
ing ideas.

Implementations of commercial versions do exist, but gener-
ally rely on computationally intensive Deep Learning Optical Character
Recognition (OCR) and huge transformer models (e.g., BERT-Large),
which demand the support of a GPU, which many academic settings
do not have.

This paper introduces CASSI-Lite (Concept-Aware Struc-
tural and Semantic Indexing Lightweight Edition), a recently developed
resource aware architecture which can be executed in full on the stan-
dard student laptops (CPU-only).

The architecture integrates a Tesser-
act OCR pipeline with an adaptive thresholding text extraction system
of image-embedded text with MiniLM embedding system and quantiza-
tion of text semantics.

It is also proposed that a novel Hybrid Similarity
Metric should be used that is a combination of overlap, concept graph
intersection, and structural similarity.

Extensive testing of a new evasion
dataset demonstrates that CASSI-Lite is capable of detecting image-
based evasion of plagiarism with 90% accuracy, with an AI-paraphrased
text at high 80% accuracy, and with a latency of only a few seconds per
page at an inference performance on a typical student laptop.

Keywords: Plagiarism Detection · Optical Character Recognition · Nat-
ural Language Processing · Resource-Efficient Computing · AI Para-
phrasing · Academic Integrity
1
Introduction
The belief of academic integrity is what supports educational and research insti-
tutions.

However, the technological the plagiarism landscape has changed radi-
cally within the past ten years.

The customary paradigm of copy-paste plagiarism
2
Anshu Kumar, Anirban Dutta, Purushottam Choudhary, and Amit Seth
has taken a new appearance as smart avoidance [1].

There are two major vectors
involved in this shift (1) Format Obfuscation, where text is encoded as an image
(e.g.

scans, screenshots) to circumvent text parsers and (2) Generative Obfus-
cation, in which AI programs such as ChatGPT or Quillbot are used to rewrite
text to change syntax, but not semantics [2].

AI detection has been integrated into existing commercial solutions, like Tur-
nitin or iThenticate features.

These systems are however, usually run as propri-
etary cloud based systems with restricted algorithmic transparency which is
served by cloud infrastructure and poses privacy issues and needs subscription
based deployment models.

On the other hand, the implementation of open-source
research is often based on the state-of-the-art models such as TrOCR [3] or
RoBERTa-Large [4].
GPUs for inference.

This brings about a resource gap in
which smaller institutions or individual evaluators is unable to install intensive
detection systems on the ordinary hardware.

CASSI-Lite is planned to be a localized, deep analysis plagiarism detector of
academic submissions, e.g.
assignments, reports, and theses.

It is not configured
as a web-scale crawler or an alternative to business cloud-hosted plagiarism
databases, but as an open and resources-saving solution use as an institution
and as an individual.

The rest of the paper is organized in the following manner:
Section 2 reviews related work.
In section 3, the problem is defined formally.
The CASSI-Lite methodology is described in Section 4.

Section 5 outlines the
implementation and its limitations.

Experimental results are given in section 6,
preceded by a summary of the results by discussion and conclusions.

2
Related Work
2.1
Traditional and Semantic Plagiarism Detection
Early detection algorithms were based on string matching algorithms such as
Rabin-Karp and suffix trees [6].

While they are efficient, and do not resist simple
replacement of synonyms.

The Vector Space Models (VSM) were introduced and
Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) enabled certain semantic matching [7], however,
the techniques tend to lose contextual nuance.

Transformer architectures are used
in recent advancements.

BERT [8] and its derivatives contain rich contextual
representations.

Nevertheless, the standard BERT models need large memory
bandwidth.
Sentence-BERT (SBERT) proposed by Reimers et al.

[9] was highly
effective semantic similarity task efficiency.

We extend this by fitting distilled
versions (MiniLM) to it that will fit within student hardware limits.

2.2
OCR in Document Analysis
The Digitalization of hardcopy documents relies on Optical Character Recog-
nition (OCR).

Traditional engines pattern matching and LSTM networks are
used in like Tesseract [10].

On the contrary, new Deep Learning approach, like
TrOCR [3], OCR is an image-to-text generation problem solved by Vision trans-
formers.

Although TrOCR has accuracy at the state of the art on handwriting,
CASSI-Lite: Plagiarism Detection
3
it cannot run its inferences in a prohibitive time for CPU-only environments.
CASSI-Lite shows that Tesseract can be very aggressive to image preprocessing.

The efficiency of act provides a superior trade-off on the analysis of academic
documents [11].

2.3
Resource-Constrained NLP and Green AI
Although the main measure of the plagiarism detection literature is accuracy, the
cost of the computation is the key issue of having state-of-the-art performance
is frequently ignored.

BERT-Base standard transformers have 110 million pa-
rameters, which need about 440 MB of memory (constituting weights only, not
the actual model).

Attention matrices during inference overhead on attention
matrices.

In resource limited settings like personal student laptops, this memory
footprint can easily cause swap usage, which reduces performance.

New mod-
els in the field of the Green AI recommend model distillation and quantization.
Techniques proposed by Wang et al.

[17] prove that knowledge distillation of a
teacher model (BERT) to a student model (MiniLM) is possible.

Semantic capa-
bility can be retained by 90% and the inference latency can be lowered 80%.

This
philosophy is taken by CASSI-Lite, contrary to the trend of using increasingly
large Large Language Models (LLMs) for detection.

We conform by only adher-
ing to architectural operations that can be executed by the CPU, the principles
of the democratization of AI, that make the academic integrity tools affordable
to the institutions which have no High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters.

2.4
The Gap in Localized Deployment
The commercial APIs (e.g., GPTZero, Turnitin) are a solution to the resource
problem, which transfers the computation to the cloud.

This, however, comes
with risks of data sovereignty especially with unpublished theses or sensitive
grant proposals.

Privacy-preserving verification can only be done by local de-
ployment.

Current open-source substitutes such as Sherlock or MOSS are mostly
code-based or based on old-fashioned n-gram approaches.

CASSI-Lite fills this
gap by providing a middle ground architecture: complex enough to identify se-
mantic evasion, but simplified to the extent that it will execute locally without
depending on the internet.

3
Problem Definition
We state the Multimodal Plagiarism Detection (M-PD) problem in a non-simplified
form not as a text-matching problem, but as a Semantic Reconstruction and
Alignment problem with harsh resource limitations.

3.1
The Adversarial Evasion Landscape
A plagiarist is a contravening agent who will do whatever he can to reduce the
similarity score S between his submission Dsusp and his original source Dsource,
4
Anshu Kumar, Anirban Dutta, Purushottam Choudhary, and Amit Seth
and preserve as much semantic content as possible.

We describe this evasion
operation as evasion function E(x) which is applied to the content of the source:
Dsusp = E(Dsource)
(1)
The function E has three different, and frequently overlapping, evasion vec-
tors that classical systems can hardly deal with all in unison:
Vector 1: Format Evasion (Efmt – The “Invisible Text” Problem):
This is a vector that attacks the parsing layer of detection systems.

The opponent
transforms the textual data T into a visualization V (e.g., screenshots, rasterized
PDFs or photos of the handwritten notes).

Efmt(T) →V,
where StandardParser(V ) = ∅
(2)
In traditional workflows (such as text extractors like pdftotext) treat such
images as binary blobs, and therefore the null set is the empty set.

The issue
of detection is to reverse this function so ParserCASSI(V ) ≈T, the successful
revelation of the invisible.

Vector 2: Generative Paraphrase Evasion (Epara): This vector is an
attack on the lexical matching layer.

The adversary, with the help of Generative
AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Quillbot), will take a sequence of words W = [w1, w2, .

.],
and the input will be converted into a new sequence W ′ so that the semantic
information (Information Gain) is the same, but the lexical overlap is minimized.

Jaccard(W, W ′) < ϵ
and
Semantics(W) ∼= Semantics(W ′)
(3)
The system should be able to see what remains even in the face of an al-
together disjointed surface vocabulary: the persistence of Ideas (Subject–Verb–
Object relationships).

Vector 3: Structural Obfuscation (Estr): This is performed by reversing
the order of arguments (e.g., by exchanging “Methodology” and “Related Work”),
passive-active voice reversals, or by mixing up different sources (so-called Mosaic
Plagiarism).

This disrupts sequence-based algorithms such as Rabin–Karp which
are sequential string matching.

3.2
The Core Detection Objective
The CASSI-Lite is aimed at acquiring a strong similarity function H(Dsusp, Dsource)
that remains unchanged by these adversarial transformations.

Mathematically
we want to fulfil the condition:
H(E(Dsource), Dsource) ≥τplag
(4)
in which τplag represents the decision threshold.

This would require the sys-
tem to reconstruct the underlying concept graph of a document, whether it was
displayed as an image, rewritten text or an ordered argument.

CASSI-Lite: Plagiarism Detection
5
3.3
The Resource Constraint Boundary
This problem definition is unique because of the constraint envelope.

In contrast
to commercial cloud APIs which can be scaled on demand, CASSI-Lite has
limited capabilities which are required to fit the rigid constraints of a typical
student laptop, indicated as Slaptop:
Costcompute(H) ≤Slaptop
(5)
This imposes three hard boundaries:
– Memory Wall: The entire inference process (OCR model and NLP embed-
dings) should be able to fit into approximately 4 GB RAM to create space
for the OS, excluding the option of using State-of-the-Art (SOTA) models,
such as RoBERTa-Large or TrOCR.

– Compute Wall: The entire matrix operation can and should be performed
using a CPU (AVX2 instruction set) and not GPU acceleration, requiring
model quantization.

– Latency Wall: Processing time t should be linear with document length N
in order to be self-checking with a goal of less than 5 seconds per page.

4
Proposed Methodology
The CASSI-Lite architecture is a four stage and modular pipeline architecture
that is meant to maximize the information recovery and reduce the number of
floating-point run time operations (FLOPs).

4.1
Phase 1: OCR-Based Text Recovery Module
This This module is the major line of defense against Efmt evasion.

We use
heuristic filter instead of feeding all pages to the OCR engine which is slow.

Image Filtration and Preprocessing The system analyzes the structure of the
document (XML/DOM of DOCX/PDF).

Pictures are pulled out and assessed
using a Text-Likelihood Score (λ):
λ = w1 · Contrast + w2 · EdgeDensity
(6)
Images with λ > τimg are reported as suspicious.

These pictures are prepro-
cessed with a strong lightweight OpenCV chain in order to make them Tesseract
optimized.

Adaptive Morphological Filtering Raw binary thresholding is used to filter scanned
documents when the paper is unevenly lit or when the paper grain causes uneven
lighting.

In order to reduce this without the use of heavy GPU-based denoisers,
we used a custom morphological pipeline.

We will call a structural element K as
6
Anshu Kumar, Anirban Dutta, Purushottam Choudhary, and Amit Seth
a 2×2 rect kernel.

Ibin is an image which undergoes a special opening operation
to eliminate noise (stray pixels) but leave the strokes of the characters:
Iclean = (Ibin ⊖K) ⊕K
(7)
Where ⊖denotes erosion and ⊕denotes dilation.

We discovered standard
3 × 3 kernel to be too aggressive and tended to cut through punctuations that
are vital in the determination of sentence boundaries.

2 × 2 kernel provided the
best trade-off in our calibration experiments with low DPI scans.

Furthermore,
we apply a Hough Transform based skew correction algorithm to align lines of
text horizontally, improving the line segmentation errors of Tesseract by about
18%.

Tesseract Integration The binary stream in the preprocessed form is given to
Tesseract 5.0 with LSTM mode.

The resultant text is standardized and added
into the raw text buffer of the document.

This is to make sure that the invisible
text can be made visible to the downstream NLP modules.

4.2
Phase 2: Concept Extraction and Representation
We leave lexical matching to overcome Epara (AI Paraphrasing).

We suppose
that the alteration of the verbs and adjectives by AI does not alter the Named
Entities and Noun Phrases (the “Concepts”) on a large scale.

We use the NLP library, spaCy (en_core_web_sm), which is optimized to use
the CPU.

The process involves:
– POS Tagging & Filtering: We make Nouns, Proper Nouns and Numerals.

– Lemmatization: Converting words to root forms (e.g., “algorithm’s” →“al-
gorithm”) to handle morphological variations.

– Synonym Normalization: Using a lightweight WordNet lookup to map com-
mon synonyms to a canonical concept (e.g., “method” →“approach”).

The document is thus represented not as a sequence of words, but as a mathe-
matical set of Concepts CD = {c1, c2, .
, ck}.

While we refer to this abstraction
as concept graphing, the current implementation employs lightweight concept
sets augmented with positional and structural cues, explicitly avoiding expen-
sive graph construction or graph isomorphism computations.

4.3
Phase 3: Lightweight Structural Similarity Modeling
Academic papers follow a predictable rhetorical structure (IMRAD: Introduc-
tion, Methods, Results, Discussion).

Plagiarists often clone this structure even
if they change the content.
We approximate structural alignment without expensive discourse parsing.
We segment the document into k bins based on normalized length.

A position-
aware vector Vstruct is generated where each element corresponds to the presence
of specific Rhetorical Cue Phrases (e.g., “we propose”, “in conclusion”, “experi-
mental setup”).

This Manhattan Distance metric is computationally negligible but effective
at detecting structural cloning.

4.4
Phase 4: Hybrid Similarity Computation
The fundamental innovation of CASSI-Lite is the collocation of different simi-
larity cues.

There are four independent measures, which we calculate:
– Lexical Overlap (Slex): 3-gram Jaccard Similarity.

Quick and efficient in
copy-pasting.
– Semantic Similarity (Ssem): We take all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model.

It is a
sparse Transformer (22M parameters instead of the 110M of BERT) that
can be executed efficiently on CPUs.

We calculate document embedding
Cosine Similarity.

– Concept Intersection (Scon): The Tversky Index of the mined Concept
Sets, with a weight assigned to penalizing removal of concepts, as opposed
to penalizing addition of concepts, in the mined Concept Sets.
– Structural Alignment (Sstr): According to the definition given above.

The Final Similarity Score H is a weighted linear combination:
H(A, B) = αScon + βSstr + γSsem + δSlex
(9)
Members of a validation set are empirically tuned to obtain weights: α =
0.35 (Concept), β = 0.15 (Structure), γ = 0.30 (Semantic), δ = 0.20 (Lexical).

Semantic and Concept metrics are robust in the way they are guaranteed to be
of high weight against AI paraphrasing.

5
Implementation Details
5.1
Software Stack
The system is established using Python 3.9.

The libraries are a manifestation of
the philosophy of the Lite:
– OCR Engine: Tesseract-OCR v5.3.0 (C++ backend for speed).
– Image Processing: OpenCV-Python-Headless (reduced binary size).
– NLP Core: spaCy en_core_web_sm pipeline.

– Embeddings: ONNX runtime based Sentence-Transformers to run faster on
a CPU.
– Web Framework: Streamlit as a user interface.

8
Anshu Kumar, Anirban Dutta, Purushottam Choudhary, and Amit Seth
5.2
Resource-Aware Algorithms
In order to avoid student laptop memory overflows (which frequently can be only
8 GB of RAM):
– Generator Patterns: The processing of documents by reading and processing
them as streams instead of putting the entire text in memory.

– Quantization: The MiniLM model is int8-quantized to cut the model size by
more than half (90 MB to around 23 MB) with insignificant loss in accuracy.

– Caching: The documents of the repository are pre-computed and stored as
FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) indices on disk which are loaded only
required clusters into RAM.

5.3
Optimization Strategies for Standard Hardware
To ensure stable CPU-only inference on student laptops, CASSI-Lite employs
dynamic throttling and model quantization.

OCR workers are rate-limited under
sustained high CPU utilization to prevent thermal throttling, ensuring consistent
throughput.

The MiniLM model is dynamically quantized using ONNX Runtime
(FP32 to INT8), reducing the model size from 90 MB to 22.5 MB with a neg-
ligible semantic accuracy loss (≈0.04 cosine shift).

These optimizations ensure
peak RAM usage remains below 500 MB.

End-to-End Processing Pipeline CASSI-Lite processes a suspicious document by
extracting raw text and embedded images, selectively applying OCR to suspi-
cious images, and merging recovered text into a unified representation.

Concept
sets and semantic embeddings are computed and compared against repository
documents using a hybrid similarity function, with the maximum similarity score
determining plagiarism likelihood.

6
Results and Analysis
Experimental Setup Experiments were conducted on the Synthetic Evasion Dataset
(SED-2025), comprising 100 source documents and 400 derived variants cover-
ing direct copying, image-based evasion, AI paraphrasing, and clean documents.

All experiments were performed on a CPU-only laptop (Intel i5-1135G7, 8 GB
RAM) running Ubuntu 22.04.

Performance was evaluated using accuracy, recall,
and per-page latency.

6.1
Detection Performance
We tested the CASSI-Lite and a control TF-IDF system (common in many
lightweight checkers) and pure BERT-based system (a representation of heavy
resource consumption).

Analysis: Image Evasion: Baseline models performed disastrously since they are
unable to recognize the text.

The success of the OCR module of CASSI-Lite was
to fill this gap and reach 92.4% accuracy.

The low-resolution image where OCR

6.2
Computational Efficiency
Resource efficiency was the major objective of this research.
Mean Processing Time (Text Only): 0.45 seconds/page.
Mean Processing Time (With Images): 3.2 seconds/page.
Peak RAM Usage: 420 MB.

By comparison, the BERT-Base system needed around 2.1 GB of RAM and
8.5 seconds/page on the CPU.

CASSI-Lite has a speed of about 2.6 times faster
and consumes 5 times less memory, being fully feasible in a student laptop.

6.3
Ablation Study
In order to determine how the Hybrid Metric works, we tried the system by
turning off parts:
w/o Concept Graph: AI Detection went down by 14%.
w/o Structural: False positive on generic sections of Methods went up.

This proves that to have a balanced performance, the fusion of metrics (α,
β, γ, δ) is necessary.

6.4
Scalability Stress Test
To prove the “Lite” claim, we also tested the system with document batches of
different sizes, starting with batches of 10 pages and up to batches of 100 pages.

To detect possible leaks (according to the widespread pattern in Python-based
text processing pipelines), we also monitored the RAM delta (memory drift).

Table 2 demonstrates that memory footprint is not proportional to document
length, and our stream-based processing generator is effective.

Large documents

stabilize at 440 MB even at the top of RAM because the garbage collector is
able to recycle text buffers efficiently after analysis.

The delta between the CPU
temperature (∆◦C) and the safe operating temperature of consumer laptops
suggests that although the system is an intensive one, it does not exceed safe
operating temperatures with standard cooling.

6.5
Qualitative Error Analysis
Although it was very accurate, we tested the 7.6 percent of cases in which Image
Evasion was not reported.

Low-resolution screenshots (< 96 DPI) was the major
mode of failure.

In such instances, the LSTM engine at Tesseract did not recog-
nize characters, and it had to produce howitzerlike chains.

These garbage strings
never matched to any valid nouns in the repository since our system depends on
concept extraction.

In Mosaic Plagiarism, the user put a text within complicated diagrams or
charts, this became a secondary failure mode.

These were occasionally catego-
rized by the pre-processing filter as figures (not a text containing image) to
avoid noise in the OCR, which accidentally missed the text included in the im-
age.

In this regard, future iterations would require a more detailed Region of
Interest (ROI) detection algorithm (possibly with a lightweight YOLO model)
to differentiate between text blocks and chart axes.

7
Discussion
7.1
The Trade-off: Precision vs.

Accessibility
The main principle of the CASSI-Lite is that the accessibility is far more im-
portant than marginal gains in pre-cutting of the hair in academics.

Whereas
a cloud-based GPT-4 detector can potentially have 99 percent detection rates
on text that has been paraphrased by AI, its cost (> $0.03 per 1k tokens) and
privacy concerns render it unfeasible to be widely used frequently by students
to self-check or by cash strapped departments.

CASSI-Lite trades at a some-
what lower recall rate (88.6) to achieve zero marginal cost and complete data
sovereignty.

This trade-off is especially applicable to the developing countries
where the bandwidth and hardware of the internet are underdeveloped.

Pro-
hibitive barrier to academic integrity tools is its costs.

7.2
Ethical Considerations of Local AI
The implementation of surveillance devices at the local level on the devices of
the students raises ethical issues of feature creep.

The software stack that we
have built is ephemeral in nature, meaning that it does not leave any records
of documents scanned after the session closes.

This is in contrast to commercial
SaaS platforms where submissions by students are sometimes kept to be trained.
CASSI-Lite itself is based upon a read-forget basis.

This architecture not just
CASSI-Lite: Plagiarism Detection
11
saves storage space, but is in line with GDPR principles of the Right to be
Forgotten, which promotes a relationship of trust between the institution and
the student.

7.3
Current Limitations
Multi-column scientific articles with integrated floats (figures/tables) interfere
with reading sequence.

Complicated layouts frequently lead to the creation of a
text salad, with sentences of neighboring columns mixed and semantic coherence
destroyed in the MiniLM model.

Handwriting Recognition: The LSTM engine of Tesseract is effective on
printed text, but it has performance issues with handwriting.

High loss of accu-
racy (recall less than 40) in cursive handwriting compared to transformer-based
OCR solutions like TrOCR.

Adversarial Attacks: The system is susceptible to invisible character attacks,
where whitespace characters of length zero divide n-gram tokens.

While visual
rendering is unchanged, the underlying stream of bytes is modified, circumvent-
ing lexical and exact-match filters.

Cross-Lingual Plagiarism: The existing concept extraction pipeline is lan-
guage intensive in English special POS tagging and WordNet searches.

It does
not identify plagiarism that has been translated (e.g., German source – English
submission).

7.4
Future Research Directions
Lightweight Layout Analysis: In upcoming work, we will combine a quantized
LayoutLM-v3-Tiny to solve reading order ambiguity in multi-column PDFs with-
out high compute cost.

Cross-Lingual Embeddings: To improve the English-only MiniLM, we will
use LaBSE-Lite.

Language-agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding would allow
detection of translated zero-shot plagiarism in 15+ other major languages.

Graph-Based Semantic Verification: Future iterations will build actual Knowl-
edge Graphs (KGs) in which edges are semantic relationships (e.g., “Method” –
“Algorithm”).

Graph isomorphism algorithms can then compare the structure of
ideas of two papers.

Federated Learning for Privacy: Institutions could share plagiarism finger-
prints without revealing student data.

Local cases of CASSI-Lite would train
on private repositories and only send encrypted gradient updates to a central
server.

8
Conclusion
This essay provided the design and development of CASSI-Lite, which is a frame-
work of plagiarism detection performance optimized to resources constrained
12
Anshu Kumar, Anirban Dutta, Purushottam Choudhary, and Amit Seth
surroundings.

By moving away the emphasis of raw model size to algorithmic ef-
ficiency, we have managed to confront the issues of multimodal evasion (images)
and AI paraphrasing.

The system is efficient with the current CPU hardware
enabling developing institutions or of small funds to control academic integrity
in practice.

The Hybrid Similarity metric that is proposed provides a subtle
comprehension of similarity of content and outgrows the matching of text to a
deeper, concept-conscious analysis.
